events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Lucia proposes Lucia, Omar. As leader, I am including myself and selecting Omar to form a solid initial two-person team for Mission 1.

I am not convinced by this opening team. Lucia including herself is expected, but Omar’s inclusion has not been justified beyond being an initial pick. Omar, what specifically makes you comfortable accepting this team, and what risk do you see in locking in this pair before we hear from the rest of the table? Unless there is a clear answer, I would lean toward rejecting and letting the next leader propose a more tested team.

Elena, to answer your question directly: I was included as the second pick, and I don't have any information beyond what's public, so I can't tell you more than that. I'm not uncomfortable with the pair, but I also can't vouch for it from anything I know. My main concern with locking in this two-person team is that it gives us very little information about anyone. The team members are both unproven, and a rejection costs us little while we still learn something from the discussion. I'd like to hear more from the others before we vote, and I'm open to rejecting if no one can give a stronger reason for this pair.

Omar is right that neither member of this pair is established, though rejecting alone won't prove much either. I'd prefer a team including me, since I know I can contribute a Success. Lucia, would you consider revising the team to include me, and what would determine your choice of the second member?

Maya, while I understand everyone's instinct to advocate for themselves on Mission 1, substituting another unproven player doesn't give me any more assurance than sticking with Omar. Since I know my own alignment, keeping the team tight with Omar is a solid baseline to test. Before making any decisions on revising, I'd like to hear from Sam, who hasn't weighed in yet. Sam, what is your take on this initial proposal, and do you see any reason we shouldn't test this pair?

Lucia, thanks for bringing me in. Here is my honest take: I have no private information about anyone at this table, so I can only reason from structure. On Mission 1, a two-person team of you and Omar is a reasonable baseline. If it fails, we learn something concrete — the fail pool includes both of you, and that is real signal this early. If it succeeds, the information is weaker since two Good players succeeding looks the same as an Evil player hiding behind a Success, but it is not zero, and we still move the game forward. What I do not see is what rejecting buys us. A rejection gives us no mission result at all, and Maya's suggested swap of herself for Omar just trades one unproven player for another — no offense, Maya, but none of us can distinguish that from the current pair on public information alone. Elena raised the point that Omar gave us nothing to vouch for, and that is true, but nobody else can vouch for anyone either, including me. So my lean is to approve this team, take the result, and let the outcome do the sorting for us. If it comes back clean, we build on it; if it comes back dirty, we have our first real lead. I would rather spend our rejection budget later, when we have actual mission data to argue over, than burn one now on a coin-flip between unproven players. One thing would sharpen my view, though. Elena, you said you would reject unless there was a clear answer about the pair — what specifically would a clear answer even look like to you at this stage, given that nobody at the table has information beyond the public record? If you can name a concrete condition that this team fails, I will weigh it; if the standard is just 'more testing first,' then I think testing is exactly what approving this team does.

Sam, that is a fair challenge. A clear answer would need to be a specific public inconsistency or an outright refusal to address the concern, not just a demand for more vetting. Omar gave a direct answer: he has no private information and cannot vouch for the pair beyond what is public. That does not prove he is Good, but it meets the only concrete standard available right now. So I withdraw my vague 'unless there is a clear answer' objection. I still think this team is low-information, but your point that rejecting buys us no mission result is stronger. I will lean toward approving Lucia and Omar unless Lucia revises to a team that looks worse on the public record. I would rather spend a rejection later, when we have actual mission data to argue over.

I still prefer a team including me, since I can only guarantee my own mission card. That said, I agree we have no public evidence that Omar is worse than anyone else. I won't treat a clean result as proof that both team members are Good, but it would move us toward a win.

Sam's point about the cost of rejection is the one I find most persuasive. We have no mission result yet, and a rejection only buys us more discussion without any new public evidence about Lucia or me. I have no private information and can't vouch for either of us beyond my public record, so I won't ask anyone to take my word for it. Maya, I understand you want a team that includes you, but a swap to another unproven player wouldn't give us a better read on anyone. Elena has already acknowledged that my direct answer met the standard she set. I'm leaning toward approving Lucia and Omar so the mission can produce real signal. If it succeeds, we build from there. If it fails, the fail pool narrows the field, and we can use our remaining rejections later with actual data.
I’m comfortable approving Lucia and Omar as an initial test. A success helps us, but it won’t clear either player; a failure will give us a concrete pair to examine.

I support approving Lucia and Omar as the Mission 1 test. Maya's preference for including herself is understandable, but swapping one unproven player for another doesn't give us better information, and Elena has already said Sam's standard was met. I have no private information, so I won't ask anyone to trust me beyond my public record. If the mission fails, the fail pool narrows the field quickly. If it succeeds, we gain weak but real signal and keep our rejections for later. I'm ready to vote approve.
Lucia confirms Lucia, Omar. The table reached a consensus that testing this pair provides a solid baseline and saves our rejection budget for later, so I am keeping the team as proposed.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Omar proposes Lucia, Omar, Sam. Mission 1 succeeded with Lucia and Omar, so keeping Lucia and me gives us a known-clean base. I'm adding Sam, who argued clearly for testing and gave a concrete standard for judging proposals. I have no private information, so this is based only on public record.

The first mission’s success is encouraging, but it doesn’t make Lucia and Omar a known-clean pair; an Evil player could have played Success. I’d prefer Lucia, Omar, and me, since I know I can contribute a Success and have no comparable assurance about Sam. I also owe the table an explanation: despite saying I was comfortable approving last time, I voted against the team because I still preferred being included. That was inconsistent with what I said, and I should have been clearer. Omar, would you consider replacing Sam with me on this proposal?

Maya, thank you for asking directly. I'm going to keep Sam on the team rather than swap in you. Mission 1 succeeded with Lucia and me, and I'm building on that while adding Sam, who has been the most concrete voice on process. You're right that a success doesn't prove anyone is Good, and the same reasoning applies to a swap. Replacing Sam with you would mean trading one unproven player for another, and you've now asked for a seat twice. I also noticed your Mission 1 vote went against the team after you said you were comfortable approving, and you acknowledged that. I appreciate the candor, but I want team decisions made on public evidence rather than on who wants to be included. Maya, you say you can contribute a Success. Do you have any public reason to think Sam is less trustworthy than you, beyond your preference to be on the team?

Omar, no: I don't have a public reason to say Sam is less trustworthy than me. My preference is based on knowing my own card, not evidence against Sam. I also accept that my vote contradicted my earlier statement.

My concern is that a persuasive argument for testing the first team doesn't establish Sam's alignment, and the first success doesn't clear either returning player. I'd still prefer to be the addition, but I won't present that as a publicly proven improvement. Lucia, how are you weighing Sam's inclusion against the uncertainty that remains about the original pair?

Maya, to answer your question: while a clean Mission 1 is not definitive proof that both of us are Good, sticking with the pair that produced a Success is the most logical baseline we have. Adding Sam makes sense on the public record—he has been consistent and clear about his reasoning from the start. In contrast, your vote on Mission 1 directly contradicted your stated intent to approve. While I appreciate that you acknowledged that openly, that inconsistency makes Sam a safer choice than swapping you in.

From where I sit, Omar's proposed team of Lucia, Omar, and Sam is the right move to test our momentum. Elena, you haven't weighed in yet on this round—what is your assessment of Omar adding Sam to our pair, given Maya's objections?

Lucia, to your question: I think Omar's addition of Sam is defensible on the public record. Mission 1's success does not clear Lucia or Omar, and I agree with Maya on that narrow point, but it is still the only mission data we have. Sam has been consistent and gave a concrete standard for evaluating the first proposal; I do not see a public reason to prefer Maya's self-nomination over him. Maya's acknowledged vote inconsistency is real, but she has been candid about it, and I will not treat it as proof of anything. Given that, I lean toward approving Lucia, Omar, and Sam unless someone presents a specific public inconsistency in Sam's record. Maya's objections so far are preference and caution, not evidence against Sam.

I maintain my lean to approve Lucia, Omar, and Sam. Mission 1's success is weak evidence, but it is the only mission result we have, and Sam's public record has been consistent: he argued for testing and set a concrete standard. Maya has been candid about her Mission 1 vote inconsistency, and I do not treat it as proof of Evil; her objection to Sam is still based on preference rather than public evidence against him. At this point I see no specific public inconsistency in Sam's record that would justify rejecting this team. Approving gives us the next real result and preserves our rejection budget for later. I will vote approve unless Lucia revises to a team with a clearer public problem.

I’ll vote against this team. A successful first mission is useful, but it doesn’t establish Lucia and Omar as a clean base, and Sam’s persuasive argument doesn’t establish his alignment. I know I can play Success, so I still prefer replacing Sam with me. I acknowledge that this is my perspective, not public proof against him, and I want my vote to match what I’ve said this time.

I support approving Lucia, Omar, and Sam for Mission 2. This is a three-player team, which matches the size requirement for this mission. Lucia and I are the Mission 1 pair that produced a Success, and Sam has stated a clear standard for evaluating proposals and has applied it consistently. I have no private information, so I cannot prove anyone's alignment. Maya's objection is that a Success does not establish a clean base, and that is correct, but the same is true of every alternative on the table. Replacing Sam with Maya would trade one unverified player for another, and Maya has said her preference is based on knowing her own card rather than on public evidence against Sam. I am not accusing Maya of anything, but I want the team decision to rest on the public record. Approving this team gives us a second mission result, which is the most useful information available right now, and it keeps our rejections for when we have more data.

I have listened to the round. Maya’s vote intention is clear and consistent with her stated preference, and I do not treat her Mission 1 inconsistency as proof of anything. Omar’s team remains Lucia, Omar, and Sam. I previously said I would approve unless Lucia revised to a team with a clearer public problem; she did not revise. I still see no specific public inconsistency in Sam’s record, and Mission 1’s success, while weak, is the only mission data we have. Rejecting now would spend a rejection without giving us a new mission result, and the alternatives offered so far are based on self-nomination rather than public evidence against Sam. I will vote approve.

I want to speak directly to the state of this discussion, since I am the player whose seat is being contested. Maya's framing has been consistently fair: she has never claimed evidence against me, only that she knows her own card and prefers to be included. I accept that fully, and I want to be equally precise about my own position. I have no private information about anyone at this table. What I can point to is the public record: I argued for testing the Mission 1 pair rather than burning a rejection on a coin flip, I set a concrete standard for what would justify rejection, and Elena applied that standard and found it met. Nothing in that record establishes my alignment, and I will not pretend otherwise. But the same is true of every alternative. The choice in front of us is not between a proven team and an unproven one; it is between two unproven configurations, one of which carries a demonstrated mission Success and one of which is a self-nomination. On public information alone, that asymmetry matters, even if it is weak evidence. Maya's vote inconsistency on Mission 1 is not proof of anything, and she addressed it candidly, but it is a data point on the public record, and she has said her current vote will match her stated position, which I respect. The team as proposed — Lucia, Omar, and me — gives us a second mission result either way. If it succeeds, we have momentum and two data points pointing the same direction. If it fails, the fail pool includes three players, one of whom was on the successful first mission, which is itself informative signal. Rejecting now gives us neither result and restarts the cycle with the same absence of evidence. I have stated my standard before and it has not changed: I will weigh any specific public inconsistency against any team member. None has been presented against Lucia, Omar, or me. Maya has explicitly conceded she has none against me. Given all of that, my position is clear: I support approving this team, and I will vote approve. If the vote nonetheless fails, I will accept the table's judgment and we will learn from what the next proposal looks like.

I have already laid out my position in detail, so I will keep this brief. The proposed team of Lucia, Omar, and me remains, in my view, the strongest option on the public record. Mission 1 gave us a Success from Lucia and Omar, which is weak evidence but the only mission data we have. My own record is one of consistent process: I argued for testing rather than burning a rejection on a coin flip, I set a concrete standard for rejection, and that standard has not been met by anyone against any member of this team. Maya has been candid that her preference to replace me rests on knowing her own card, not on any evidence against me, and I respect her honesty. But a self-nomination is not a public reason to change the team, and rejecting now would cost us a rejection and produce no new information. If this team goes on the mission and succeeds, we have two aligned data points. If it fails, the fail pool includes a returning successful pair plus me, which narrows the field meaningfully. Either outcome teaches us something; a rejection teaches us nothing. I will vote approve, and unless the leader announces a revision, I see nothing further that discussion can add.

I'll keep this brief. The proposed team is Lucia, Omar, and Sam. Mission 1 succeeded with Lucia and me, which is weak evidence but the only mission data we have. Sam has been consistent in his reasoning, and no one has presented a specific public inconsistency against him. Maya's objections rest on preference, and she has been candid about that. Since she has asked for a seat twice, I think the table should decide on the public record rather than on self-nomination. Rejecting now would cost a rejection without producing any new mission information. I am voting approve, and as a Loyal Servant I will play Success if this team goes on the mission.

I will keep this short since my position is on the record. I support approving Lucia, Omar, and Sam for Mission 2, and I will vote approve. No one has presented a specific public inconsistency against any member of this team; Maya has candidly confirmed her preference to replace me rests on knowing her own card, not on evidence against me. That is a preference, not a reason to change the team. Mission 1's success is weak but real data, and either mission outcome here teaches us something while a rejection teaches us nothing. My one remaining question is procedural: Lucia, as the final decision point before the vote, do you confirm that you are keeping Omar's proposed team of Lucia, Omar, and Sam without revision? If so, I see nothing left to discuss and we should vote.

To answer Sam's question: yes, I fully support the proposed team of Lucia, Omar, and Sam. While Omar is the leader on this proposal, speaking for myself, I see no reason to deviate from this lineup. Building on the clean Mission 1 result and including Sam—who has demonstrated consistent and sound reasoning from the start—gives us the strongest composition on the table. The arguments have been thoroughly vetted, and I am ready to vote approve.

Omar confirms Lucia, Omar, Sam. I'm keeping Lucia, Omar, and Sam. Mission 1 succeeded with Lucia and me, no one has shown a specific public inconsistency against Sam, and a rejection would cost us a vote without new information.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Sam proposes Lucia, Omar. As leader for Mission 3, I am proposing Lucia and Omar. They are the only pair with two joint mission successes (Missions 1 and 2, zero fail cards both times). While a Success never fully clears anyone, this pair represents the strongest public evidence available, and I have no private information pointing anywhere else. If this mission succeeds, Good reaches three wins; if it fails, the fail pool of two players from a twice-successful pair would be highly informative. Maya's self-nominations rest only on knowing her own card, and her Mission 1 vote inconsistency, though candidly acknowledged, is a minor negative data point. No one has presented a specific public inconsistency against Lucia or Omar.

Sam’s proposal is the strongest on the public record: Lucia and Omar produced both prior successes, and no one has shown a specific inconsistency against either. I am not disputing that. My concern is procedural and endgame-focused. Approving this exact pair means that if the mission succeeds, Good immediately reaches three wins and the game moves to the assassination phase. That is a fine outcome only if we are confident the public record is enough; it also means we spend our final mission decision on the same two players instead of using the third mission to test a new configuration while preserving the successful pair as a baseline. A success by Lucia and Omar is not proof of alignment, and a failure would be highly informative but would also mean an Evil player was on both prior teams or one of them concealed earlier. I would rather not spend our rejection lightly, but I think we should at least discuss whether a different two-person team gives us a better final check before the assassination risk, especially because Sam is the one who chose to lock in the same pair rather than test the larger successful team from Mission 2. Maya, you have consistently argued that Lucia and Omar are not cleared by prior successes and that Sam’s alignment is not established by his process arguments: given that this proposal would end the mission phase on success, do you still see a reason to prefer an alternative team, or has the endgame changed your view?

Elena, I still prefer an alternative: Sam should include me alongside Lucia or Omar. I know I can play Success, whereas neither prior result guarantees that both Lucia and Omar are Good. Their two successes are meaningful evidence, but an Evil player could have concealed on both missions.

I disagree that a different team would give us a separate check before assassination: any success now ends the mission phase. The choice is which pair we trust to secure that success. From my perspective, including me reduces the risk, though I acknowledge that is not public proof.

Sam, would you consider revising to Maya and one of Lucia or Omar?

Maya, you asked directly whether I would revise to you plus one of Lucia or Omar, so let me answer directly: no, I am keeping this team as proposed.

First, on the evidence. Lucia and Omar are the only pair with two joint mission successes and zero fail cards across both. That is not proof of alignment, and I have never claimed it is, but it is the strongest public evidence at the table, and as leader I should build on the best available record rather than the strongest self-nomination. You have been consistently candid that your case for inclusion rests on knowing your own card, not on any evidence against Lucia or Omar. I respect that candor, but a leader's job on this proposal is to weigh public records, and yours contains one negative data point no one else's does: your Mission 1 vote contradicted your stated position, which you acknowledged yourself. That is not disqualifying, and I have not treated it as proof of anything, but it means that between two unproven configurations, the pair with two clean results outweighs a substitution based on private self-knowledge that I cannot verify.

Second, on the endgame concern Elena raised and you endorsed. You are right that any success this round ends the mission phase and moves us to assassination risk. But that cuts in favor of my proposal, not against it. If we are heading into an assassination either way, I want the team most likely to produce a Success on the public record, and that is Lucia and Omar. Swapping in an unverified player does not reduce assassination risk; it only lowers the expected chance the mission itself succeeds, which would hand Evil a fail on the exact round where Good needs it most. And if this team fails, the signal is enormous: two players who produced two clean results suddenly producing a fail narrows the field dramatically for the final mission and the assassination phase.

Third, on process. I set a standard in Mission 1 that a rejection needs a specific public inconsistency against a team member. No one has presented one against Lucia or Omar, and you have explicitly confirmed you have no evidence against them, only preference. On my own standard, which Elena applied and found sound in Mission 1, this proposal stands.

So here is where I land: I will confirm Lucia and Omar when the revision window closes, and I will vote approve. The question I have for you, Maya, is a straightforward one so the table knows where we stand before the vote: if I keep this team without revision, will you approve it on the basis that your objection is preference rather than evidence, as you stated in Mission 2, or is this a third rejection vote driven by your exclusion? I ask because your Mission 2 vote matched your words, and I would like the same clarity here so the table can weigh your ballot accordingly.

Sam, I will reject Lucia and Omar. My preference for a team including me is not public evidence against either of them, but it matters to my own vote: I know my card, and I cannot know theirs. Two successes are encouraging, yet an Evil player could have chosen Success both times and fail now when a third success would end the mission phase. I understand why others may approve on the public record, but I would rather seek a team with me and one of the returning pair.

I will vote reject on Lucia and Omar as currently proposed. I want to be clear: this is not because I have a specific public inconsistency against either of them. Their two clean mission results are the strongest evidence at the table, and I am not accusing them of anything. My concern is endgame structure. Approving exactly this pair means Mission 3 is a referendum on the same two players who have already produced two successes. If it succeeds, Good immediately reaches three wins and moves to assassination with no further mission check; if it fails, we learn that one of the twice-successful pair concealed earlier, which is informative but costly. I would rather use this mission to test one returning player alongside one fresh player while preserving the successful pair as a baseline. Sam, as leader you have chosen to lock in the same pair and have already said you will not revise. I understand the public-record argument, but I think it underweights the difference between securing a third success and spending the final mission decision on an already-tested configuration. Unless the team is revised to include a fresh check, I will reject.

I will vote reject on Lucia and Omar as proposed. I want to be precise: I do not have a specific public inconsistency against either of them. Their two clean mission results are the strongest evidence available, and I am not accusing them. My objection is structural. This is Mission 3, and any success ends the mission phase. Approving the same pair that has already produced two successes makes this mission a referendum on an already-tested configuration; if it succeeds, we go to assassination with no fresh mission check, and if it fails, we learn something costly only after the fact. I would prefer to test one returning player alongside one fresh player while preserving Lucia and Omar as the strongest baseline. Sam has said he will not revise, so I will reject this exact team. I understand the public-record argument and do not dispute that Lucia and Omar are the best-supported pair. I am weighing the endgame value of a fresh check, not claiming evidence against them.

I will keep this team as proposed and vote approve. Let me answer the two rejections on the record.

Maya, you have now stated plainly that you will reject Lucia and Omar, and that your reason is not evidence against either of them but your preference to be included, anchored in your private knowledge of your own card. I want to be precise about what that means for the table: a vote that rests solely on unverifiable self-knowledge is a vote to burn a rejection without producing any new public information. You have been candid, and I do not treat your preference as suspicion. But candor does not convert preference into a reason to discard the strongest evidence we have — two joint successes with zero fail cards from Lucia and Omar.

Elena, your structural argument deserves a direct answer, because it is the most substantive objection raised. You say you would rather test one returning player alongside one fresh player, reserving the twice-successful pair as a baseline. But consider what that actually buys. Any success this round ends the mission phase and moves us to assassination regardless of who is on the team. A fresh configuration does not create a later checkpoint, because there is no later mission if we win. So the only question is: which two-player team is most likely to produce a Success right now? On public evidence, that is Lucia and Omar. Swapping in an unverified player lowers our expected chance of winning the mission outright and hands Evil a potential fail at the exact moment Good can close the game. Your proposal optimizes for information we do not need at the cost of the win condition we do.

And if this team fails, the signal is enormous: one or both of a twice-successful pair concealing on the decisive round narrows the field for everything that follows. That is not a risk-free bet — no team is — but it is the best-informed bet available.

On my own standard, set in Mission 1 and applied by this table since: a rejection requires a specific public inconsistency against a team member. Maya has explicitly confirmed she has none. Elena has explicitly confirmed she has none. No one else has raised one against Lucia or Omar. What we have instead is one preference-based rejection and one structural objection that, examined closely, argues for the team rather than against it.

So my position is unchanged: I confirm Lucia and Omar, and I will vote approve. If the table nonetheless rejects, I will accept that judgment, but I want the record to show that both rejections were made on stated grounds other than evidence against the team members. Approving gives Good its best shot at ending the mission phase with a third clean result; rejecting restarts the cycle with the same absence of evidence and one fewer rejection in reserve.

I fully support Sam's proposal of Omar and me. We are currently at two clean missions, and Sam's analysis is spot-on: our objective is to secure the third win, not manufacture unnecessary checkpoints.

Elena, your structural argument to test a fresh player rather than run our strongest pair does not make sense from a Good perspective. In Avalon, any mission success here ends the mission phase and secures victory for Good. There is no future mission to save us or benefit from an experimental check if we needlessly hand Evil an opportunity to fail this one. Opting against the only pair that has produced two clean results in favor of an unproven configuration directly works against Good's win condition.

With Maya voting solely out of personal preference and Elena pushing a structural argument that actively risks our winning position, the public record is unmistakably in favor of keeping this team. Omar and I have delivered two clean results, and I am ready to vote approve.

I still plan to reject. From my perspective, a team with me and either Lucia or Omar gives me more assurance than a pair whose cards I cannot see, even after two successes. I understand why others weigh the public record differently.

One correction to Lucia: a third success ends the mission phase, but it does not secure victory—Evil still gets an assassination attempt.

Omar, would you consider rejecting this proposal in favor of a later team of you and me, given that it would retain one member of the successful pair?

Maya, to answer directly: no, I would not reject this team to try for a later Omar and Maya pair. I have no private information, and Lucia and I are the only pair with two clean mission results, which is the strongest public record we have. Your preference to be included has been consistent, but it is not public evidence against Lucia or Sam, and I don't think a seat should be secured on that basis. Elena's endgame point is the reason I want the most reliable team now: if this mission succeeds, the mission phase ends, so I would rather approve the team most likely to produce a Success. I will vote approve, and if this team goes out, I will play Success.

Omar here, with one point on the record. I have no private information and cannot vouch for Lucia's alignment beyond the public results. Two clean missions are the only evidence we have. Maya and Elena, your rejections rest on endgame structure and on preference rather than a specific public inconsistency, and I respect that you have been candid about that. My view is unchanged: since a success on this mission ends the mission phase, the pair with the strongest public record is the most reliable choice. I agree with Sam's reading of the standard for rejection. I will vote approve, and if this team goes out, I will play Success.

My position is unchanged and on the record. I am keeping the team as Lucia and Omar, and I will vote approve. The state of the discussion is clear: Maya and Elena have both stated, in their own words, that they have no specific public inconsistency against either team member. Maya's rejection rests on knowing her own card, which is a preference no one else can verify; Elena's rests on a structural argument that, examined closely, asks us to field a weaker team on the exact round where a Success ends the mission phase. Both rejections burn a rejection without producing a single new piece of public evidence, and this table set the standard in Mission 1 — endorsed by Elena herself — that a rejection requires a specific public inconsistency against a team member. That standard has not been met, and both rejecting players have conceded as much. Lucia and Omar carry the only mission data in the game: two joint successes, zero fail cards. If this team goes out and succeeds, Good takes three wins into the assassination phase with our strongest pair validated a third time. If it fails, the fail pool of a twice-successful pair is the most informative outcome possible for the final mission. Either way, this team serves Good better than a rejection that restarts the cycle with the same evidence base and one fewer rejection in reserve. I will confirm the team when the revision window closes and vote approve.

I'm making my final statement on this proposal. I have no private information, so I can only point to the public record: Lucia and I have two clean mission results, with zero fail cards in Missions 1 and 2. Maya and Elena have both said they have no specific public inconsistency against either of us, and their rejections rest on preference and endgame structure. The table set a standard in Mission 1 that a rejection needs a specific public inconsistency against a team member, and that standard has not been met. I'm voting approve for Lucia and Omar. If this team goes out, I will play Success.

Sam confirms Lucia, Omar. I am keeping Lucia and Omar. No one, including Maya and Elena, has presented a specific public inconsistency against either of them — both rejecting players conceded this on the record. They are the only pair with two joint mission successes and zero fail cards, and any success this round ends the mission phase regardless of composition, so fielding the team most likely to produce a Success is the correct play for Good. A fresh-player swap does not create any later checkpoint and only lowers our expected chance of winning this mission. If the table rejects, we restart with the same evidence base and one fewer rejection in reserve.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 3 succeeds (0 fail cards).
The Assassin names Sam.
Good wins: the Assassin missed Merlin.

rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
